name: Katana
history: The katana grew out of the older tachi, which was worn edge-down from the belt. As fighting on foot became common in the Muromachi period, samurai began wearing the blade edge-up through the sash, which let them draw and cut in one motion.
Smiths coated the spine of the blade in clay before quenching, so the edge hardened more than the back. That difference gives the katana its gentle curve and the wavy line called the hamon.
In 1876 the Haitōrei edict banned carrying swords in public, ending the katana’s role as the everyday companion of the samurai.

name: Wakizashi
history: The wakizashi is the shorter Japanese sword, with a blade between 30 and 60 cm. In the Edo period samurai wore it beside the katana as a matched pair called the daisho.
Indoors, where the long sword was left at the door, the wakizashi stayed at the belt. Townspeople were allowed to carry one while travelling, but only samurai wore the pair.

name: Longsword
history: Longsword is the modern name for the large late-medieval European sword with a grip long enough for two hands. Its straight double-edged blade could cut and thrust.

Fencing manuals from the 1300s and 1400s, including those of Fiore dei Liberi, record how it was used: cuts, thrusts, grappling at close range, and gripping the blade partway along to stab through gaps in armour.

name: Claymore
history: In Scottish Gaelic, claidheamh mòr means great sword. The two-handed Highland sword of that name was used in clan warfare from the late Middle Ages into the 1600s. Its crossguard angles toward the blade and ends in quatrefoil ornaments.
Later the word was also applied to the basket-hilted Highland broadsword, so older writing can mean either weapon.

name: Rapier
history: The rapier is a slender sword built to thrust. It developed in the 1500s as a civilian sidearm worn with everyday clothes, and its swept or cup-shaped hilt protected the hand.
Fencing masters such as Salvator Fabris published treatises around 1600 that moved sword fighting toward the point and the straight line.

name: Shamshir
history: Shamshir is the Persian word for a sword with a strongly curved, single-edged blade. It is the type that English speakers often call a scimitar.
The curve suits slashing cuts, especially from horseback. Blades were often made of crucible steel, which shows a watered pattern on the surface.

name: Gladius
history: The Romans adopted a short sword from Iberia during the Punic Wars. Legionaries used it at close range, thrusting from behind a large shield called the scutum.
Two main patterns are named after places where examples were found. The Mainz pattern has a waisted blade and a long tip. The Pompeii pattern has parallel edges and a short triangular tip.

name: Khopesh
era: Bronze Age, widely used c. 1550 to 1070 BC
history: The khopesh is a sickle-shaped bronze sword. Its curved outer edge cut, and the hooked end could catch a shield or a limb.
Egyptian armies used it in the New Kingdom, and pharaohs are shown holding it in carved reliefs. After the Bronze Age it gave way to straight iron swords.
